cards.title: Subagent Offload
cards.hook: handing work to a subagent so its material never fills the orchestrator's context

claims.text: Subagent offload sends work to a child agent, so the material it reads never enters the orchestrator's context.
It fits when the orchestrator needs only a conclusion much smaller than the material behind it.
The child cannot see the orchestrator's context, so everything it needs must be packed into the dispatch.
The orchestrator sees only the child's return, so correction means dispatching again rather than steering mid-task.
Offloading raises total execution cost, but it frees room in the orchestrator's context.
Choose the child's model deliberately, because an unset choice inherits the parent's model, effort, and price.

cards.title: Deferred Context
cards.hook: keeping a short pointer loaded and fetching bulky context only when a session needs it

claims.text: Deferred context keeps a small pointer loaded and fetches the full material only when it is needed.
Defer material that is rarely needed, and also material that is always needed but only late.
In the worked example, deferring a 3,000-token reference makes a session that never needs it about 60 times cheaper.
Cut a deferred file if you cannot name the kind of session that would fetch it.
Deferral fails when the fetch fires too rarely, or so often that it matches loading everything upfront.
Caching can shrink or reverse deferral's dollar savings, but never cuts the quality cost of unneeded loaded material.

cards.title: Heavy Agent
cards.hook: subagents that carry heavy baked-in instructions the orchestrator never loads

claims.text: A heavy agent is a subagent whose definition bakes in extensive instructions, expertise, or reference material.
The orchestrator invokes the agent by type, so the baked-in weight loads only in the subagent's window.
A heavy agent's weight is the task's whole context cost: instructions, reading, exploring, and reasoning, all in the subagent's window.
The dispatch must carry whatever the agent needs from the orchestrator's context, because the agent cannot see it.
A baked-in reference can drift out of date, and the orchestrator never sees it age.
The orchestrator's transcript shows whether it only referenced the agent or actually loaded its instructions.
